title: Crude Calculations: Why the Iran War Hasn’t Yet Caused an Oil Shock | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Despite the IEA calling the Iran war's disruption of over two billion barrels through the Strait of Hormuz the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, inflation-adjusted oil prices stayed well below past-crisis peaks and the IMF trimmed global growth only modestly to 3 percent. Vaitheeswaran argues supply-side cushions (surplus, strategic releases, bypass pipelines, shale) explain part of it, but the underappreciated story is a coordinated demand response—led by China cutting seaborne crude imports over 40 percent—that points to efficiency and electrification as the 'first fuel' for managing future shocks.

insights.claim: More than two billion barrels of oil shipments have already been disrupted this year through the Strait of Hormuz, which the IEA calls the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: The physical disruption is record-setting, so the muted price reaction—not the disruption—is the real anomaly to understand for oil positioning.
insights.quote: the International Energy Agency (IEA) calls this the “largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.”

insights.claim: Inflation-adjusted benchmark petroleum prices remain well below the peaks of the 1973-74 Arab oil embargo and 1978-79 Iranian Revolution, and today's Middle East trouble has hardly slowed global growth.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: This crisis has decoupled a record physical disruption from a macro oil shock—reason to discount reflexive stagflation analogies to the 1970s.
insights.quote: Adjusted for inflation, benchmark petroleum prices remain well below the peaks seen during past global crises.
insights.locator: But that is not the biggest story here.

insights.claim: The IMF has trimmed its outlook only modestly, now predicting 3 percent global growth this year and higher next year, on the assumption of no major escalation in the war.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: The 3 percent forecast is explicitly escalation-conditional—any major flare-up is the scenario that would break the benign macro read.
insights.locator: The International Monetary Fund has trimmed its outlook

insights.claim: Oil markets were well supplied when hostilities broke out—the IEA had projected a surplus of nearly four million barrels per day for 2026—so traders did not panic.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: The pre-war supply surplus was the first shock absorber; a tighter starting balance would have produced a very different price path.
insights.locator: The straightforward explanations come from the supply side.

insights.claim: IEA-coordinated advanced economies executed the largest-ever release of strategic petroleum stocks, some 273 million barrels, which further cooled markets.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: A 273-million-barrel coordinated release shows SPR firepower still works—but also depletes a buffer that constrains response to any next shock.
insights.quote: the largest-ever release of strategic stocks of petroleum, some 273 million barrels

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia and the UAE diverted millions of barrels per day through underutilized pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz, and U.S. shale turned the country into an abundant exporter helping lubricate global markets.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: Bypass pipelines plus U.S. shale are structural resilience built from past shocks—key reasons Hormuz risk translates less directly to price than history suggests.

themes.theme: The forgotten demand response and China

insights.claim: Conventional wisdom held that oil supply, coordinated by OPEC with Saudi Arabia as the 'central bank of oil,' can be managed faster than dispersed demand, which usually responds chaotically through price spikes, shortages, and rationing.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: The supply-manageable/demand-chaotic framework is the assumption this crisis overturned—reframing how analysts should model future energy shocks.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia, the swing producer and OPEC's kingpin, was long seen as the central bank of oil.

insights.claim: China cut seaborne crude oil imports by more than five million barrels per day through June—over 40 percent below prewar levels—without triggering economic calamity, maintaining steady GDP growth between Q1 and Q2 2026.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: China proved a large, coordinated demand cut is possible without recession—a structural change in how the biggest importer can absorb supply shocks.
insights.quote: it cut seaborne imports of crude oil by more than five million barrels per day through June—over 40 percent below prewar levels—without precipitating an economic calamity at home
insights.locator: China, with its centralized energy planning

insights.claim: China absorbed the shock by dipping into strategic reserves built when oil was cheap, leaning temporarily on domestic coal and renewables, restricting product exports, and curbing fossil-fuel demand via alternative vehicles, conservation, and public transportation.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: China's playbook—reserves plus rapid demand substitution—is a template that reduces its future oil-import vulnerability and its price sensitivity to Gulf disruptions.

insights.claim: The demand shock still hit the poorest hardest: the World Bank found the Iran war widened Bangladesh's fiscal deficit and external imbalance, while Nigeria saw fuel prices spike nearly 50 percent, intensifying inflation ahead of its 2027 election.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: The pain is concentrated in frontier/emerging importers—watch Nigerian and Bangladeshi fiscal and inflation stress as the real transmission channel.
insights.locator: The World Bank's June 2026 Global Economic Prospects report

themes.theme: Efficiency and electrification as the 'first fuel'

insights.claim: Amory Lovins's 1976 Foreign Affairs article 'Energy Strategy: The Road Not Taken?' forecast U.S. energy demand could fall to 95 quadrillion Btu by 2000—a quarter below official forecasts and widely derided—yet actual 2000 U.S. consumption was ninety-seven quads.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: A fifty-year-old demand-side forecast proved nearly exact—evidence that efficiency's potential is chronically underestimated by supply-focused forecasters.
insights.quote: The actual energy consumption for the United States in 2000 was ninety-seven quads.

insights.claim: Electrification is growing at two to three times the rate of overall global energy demand, and Chinese electric-vehicle exports soared to $9.2 billion in May, nearly 50 percent higher year-on-year, as countries sought to diversify away from volatile fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: Energy shocks are now accelerating electrification and EV demand—a durable tailwind for electrification supply chains and Chinese EV exporters.
insights.quote: exports of electric vehicles from China soared—they shot up to $9.2 billion in May, nearly 50 percent higher year-on-year
insights.locator: Electrification, a far more efficient way

insights.claim: Vaitheeswaran argues efficiency, the 'forgotten fuel,' may become what the IEA calls the 'first fuel,' making future energy shocks far easier to manage so that 'Drill, baby, drill' need not be America's only path to energy abundance.
insights.speaker: Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran
insights.so_what: A structural bull case for demand-side energy tech over supply expansion—positions efficiency and electrification as strategic hedges against Gulf-supply risk.
insights.quote: “Drill, baby, drill” need not be the United States' only path to energy abundance.
insights.locator: As electrification and related technologies spread
